newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian official says EMU criteria not in doubt.
newsitem.headline: Austrian official says EMU criteria not in doubt.

text.p: A senior Austrian official appeared on Wednesday to backtrack from saying that strict adherence to criteria for European monetary union should be secondary to economic growth and employment.

Finance ministry secretary of state Wolfgang Ruttenstorfer said his comments had referred only to the period after 1997, the year when would-be EMU members have to meet targets laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.

He made the original remarks to the daily Wirtschaftsblatt. In an interview published on Wednesday, he referred to a key Maastricht target that countries should cut their budget deficit to three percent of GDP.
"One has to keep an eye on employment and economic development. That has to take precedence to strict adherence to the three percent limit as early as in 1997," he was quoted as saying.
But Ruttenstorfer told Reuters that the Maastricht criteria for EMU (economic and monetary union) were not under discussion.

"We are talking about the speed of further consolidation after 1997, but not about the criteria," he said. "For me, the criteria are beyond doubt and Austria will meet them in 1997 as they have been laid down in the treaty."

"What I have said is that in future years we have to continue consolidating our budgets but that we have to do that in a measured way so as not to impede employment and growth," said Ruttenstorfer, who joined the ministry in January from the board of industrial group OMV.
He had referred only to Austria but said he could "imagine that this is true for this or that country as well".

The Maastricht treaty sets a range of economic targets for countries wanting to join EMU, including limiting budget deficits to three percent of GDP (gross domestic product) and public debt to 60 percent.

EMU participants will be selected in spring 1998 on the basis of their 1997 economic performance. Politicians and central bankers have insisted, however, that countries have to continue on the path of fiscal virtue once they have joined.
Ruttenstorfer said that the final choice of the members was far from clear yet.
"The adherence to the criteria will be decided upon next May by the heads of government. They will not make a mathematical but a political decision, and we'll have to wait for that," he said.

Economic experts and the European Union agree that Austria is set to meet the deficit critierion this year, even though its debt ratio is expected to overshoot the 60 percent threshold by up to nine percent.

According to a recent poll, one in two Austrians are against the single currency. Labour unions are not strictly against the project but have pressed the government to place more weight on employment issues in the run-up to EMU.

The debate about strict interpretation of the criteria has gathered pace over the past few months due to fears that Germany may miss the three percent mark this year. This has fuelled speculation about a possible delay of the EMU launch in 1999.
